# Investigation: superstitions and apartment pricing {.unnumbered}

## Conceptual investigation {.unnumbered}

Read the article [Why do buildings skip the thirteenth floor?](https://academic.oup.com/jrssig/article/21/2/16/7641894).

This is a slightly different application of the DiD design: how did the authors apply the difference-in-differences (DiD) framework to this setting?

What are other ways that the authors could have estimated the causal effect of relabeling the 13th floor on apartment prices?

## Unpacking the analysis {.unnumbered}

The data and code underlying the analysis in the article are available in [this GitHub repository](https://github.com/MadisonHardesty/13th-Floor). We can read in the data as follows:

```{r}
# Load packages and read in data
library(tidyverse)

nyc <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MadisonHardesty/13th-Floor/refs/heads/main/dataNYC.csv")
```

- Take a look at the analysis code [here](https://github.com/MadisonHardesty/13th-Floor/blob/main/13th_Floor_Analysis.Rmd) to see the methods they used and how they were implemented.

- Implement your own DiD analysis using regression models (rather than the mean differences shown in the code).

- Implement a purely matching analysis (no DiD) to estimate the causal effect and compare to your DiD results.
